items.title: Evolution of Industrial Policy (1948 → 1956 → 1991)
items.body:
**In one line** — India's industrial policy moved from a state-led, licence-controlled economy to an open, competition-driven one.

**Why it is asked** — The 1948/1956/1991 markers, the 'economic constitution' tag and the de-reservation numbers (17 → 8 → 2) are repeat one-mark facts.

## The story

- **IPR 1948** (Industrial Policy Resolution) — India's **first** industrial policy. It accepted a **mixed economy**: the state would run key industries while private firms kept a role.
- **IPR 1956** (Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956) — often called the **'economic constitution of India'**. It was framed to give effect to the **socialist pattern of society** and the **Second Five Year Plan** (the Mahalanobis model that stressed heavy industry). It sorted industries into three schedules:

| Schedule | Who develops it | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| A (17 industries) | State only — the State to be exclusively responsible for future development | Arms, atomic energy, railways |
| B | Progressively state-owned, but the private sector supplements the State | Aluminium, machine tools, fertilisers |
| C | Left to the private sector | All the rest |

- For decades firms needed a government **licence** to start, expand or change products — the **'Licence-Permit Raj'** — which bred delay and inefficiency.
- **New Industrial Policy 1991** — triggered by a **balance-of-payments crisis**, it brought **abolition of industrial licensing** for all but a small list of industries, a **reduction in the number of industries reserved exclusively for the public sector (17 to 8)**, opened the door to **FDI**, and the **replacement of the MRTP Act's pre-entry restrictions** (prior permission to expand) with a new competition framework (the **Competition Act, 2002**). This was the industrial arm of the **LPG** reforms (Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation).
- **Disinvestment:** since 1991 the Government has progressively reduced its equity in several public sector enterprises. Disinvestment (selling part of the government's shares) and **strategic privatisation** (selling control) are used to raise resources and improve enterprise efficiency; the department in charge is **DIPAM**.
- Reserved industries then fell further: **17 (1956) → 8 (1991) → 2 today** (atomic energy and railway operations).

## Terms explained

- **Mixed economy** — both government and private firms produce goods.
- **Licence-Permit Raj** — the pre-1991 system of needing permits to run industry.
- **MRTP Act** — old law curbing monopolies; replaced by the Competition Act, 2002.
- **FDI** — Foreign Direct Investment, long-term investment by overseas firms.

**Don't confuse** — **1948** (first policy, mixed economy) with **1956** (public-sector dominance, 'economic constitution'); **1991** is the liberalisation break.

**Remember it** — '48-56-91 = Foundation → Public-sector peak → Liberalisation.

**TL;DR**

- IPR 1948: first policy, mixed economy.
- IPR 1956: 'economic constitution', Schedules A/B/C, Second Plan.
- NIP 1991: delicensing + LPG; reserved industries 17 → 8 → 2 (atomic energy, railways).
- MRTP Act → Competition Act, 2002 (CCI operational 2009).
keyPoints: IPR 1948 was India's first industrial policy and set up a mixed economy.
IPR 1956 — the 'economic constitution of India' — created Schedule A (17 state-exclusive industries), B and C, tied to the Second Plan.
The New Industrial Policy 1991 abolished most industrial licensing and launched liberalisation.
1991 reduced public-sector reserved industries from 17 to 8; today only 2 remain (atomic energy, railway operations).
The MRTP Act was replaced by the Competition Act, 2002 (CCI operational 2009).
items.mnemonic: Policy years '48-56-91' = Foundation (mixed economy) → Public-sector dominance → Liberalisation.
items.source: NCERT Indian Economic Development; DPIIT industrial policy history

items.title: Classification of Industries
items.body:
**In one line** — Industries are grouped four ways — by activity, ownership, product and scale — and exams test which bucket an example falls in.

**Why it is asked** — Discrimination questions (is software 'primary' or 'quaternary'? is steel a consumer or capital good?) rely on these labels.

## The story

**By activity (the production stage):**
- **Primary** — taking resources straight from nature (agriculture, mining, forestry, fishing).
- **Secondary** — turning those into goods (steel, cement, textiles, automobiles, construction).
- **Tertiary** — services (banking, insurance, healthcare, transport, tourism).
- **Quaternary** — knowledge services (IT, R&D, consultancy).

**By ownership:** **Private** (Reliance, Tata), **Public** (IOC, BHEL), **Joint** (Maruti Suzuki, originally a government-Suzuki venture), **Cooperative** (Amul, IFFCO).

**By product type:** **Consumer goods** (bought for final use), **Capital goods** (machinery that other industries use to produce), **Intermediate goods** (inputs such as steel and chemicals).

**By scale:** **Small-scale** (low capital, labour-intensive) and **large-scale** (high capital, mass production).

## Terms explained

- **Capital goods** — machines and equipment used to make other goods (a lathe, a turbine).
- **Intermediate goods** — half-finished inputs (steel, chemicals) that go into a final product.
- **Quaternary** — the knowledge/information layer of services.

**Don't confuse** — **Mining is primary** (extraction), not quaternary; **software/IT is quaternary**, not primary; **steel used in a car is a capital/intermediate input**, not a consumer good.

**Remember it** — Activity order follows the journey of a resource: dig it (primary) → make it (secondary) → serve it (tertiary) → think it (quaternary).

**TL;DR**

- Activity: primary (extraction), secondary (manufacturing), tertiary (services), quaternary (knowledge).
- Ownership: private, public, joint (Maruti Suzuki), cooperative (Amul).
- Product: consumer, capital (machinery for others), intermediate goods.
keyPoints: By activity: primary (extraction), secondary (manufacturing), tertiary (services), quaternary (knowledge/R&D).
By ownership: private, public, joint (e.g. Maruti Suzuki) and cooperative (e.g. Amul, IFFCO).
By product: consumer goods, capital goods (machinery for other industries), intermediate goods.
Capital goods industries supply the machinery and equipment used by other industries.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Industries (classification)

items.title: Public Sector Enterprises & the Ratna Classification
items.body:
**In one line** — Government-owned companies (PSEs) come in three legal forms and earn 'Ratna' grades that decide how freely they can spend.

**Why it is asked** — PSE-type matching (Railways vs LIC vs SAIL) and the Maharatna money-thresholds are high-frequency.

## The story — why PSEs exist

PSEs were set up to speed growth in **critical sectors**, spread **balanced regional development**, create **jobs**, keep **strategic sectors** (defence, energy, transport) in state hands, and steady prices.

## Three organisational types

| Type | Feature | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Departmental undertaking | Run directly by a ministry; no separate legal identity | Indian Railways, India Post |
| Statutory corporation | Created by a special Act of Parliament | Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) |
| Government company | Registered under the Companies Act; government holds at least 51% | Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL), BHEL, NTPC |

## Ratna status (grades of spending autonomy)

- **Maharatna** (created 2010) — the top grade; can invest up to **15% of net worth (capped at ₹5,000 crore)** in one project without government approval. To qualify a firm must already hold **Navratna status**, and needs net worth of at least ₹15,000 crore, turnover of at least ₹25,000 crore and net profit of at least ₹5,000 crore** (average annual figures over the last three years).
- **Navratna** — invest up to ₹1,000 crore without approval; needs Miniratna status plus a score of at least 60 out of 100.
- **Miniratna Category-I and II** — lower autonomy for profit-making CPSEs.
- As of **2025 there are 14 Maharatnas, 26 Navratnas and 65 Miniratnas**.

## Terms explained

- **CPSE** — Central Public Sector Enterprise.
- **Net worth** — the company's own funds (share capital + reserves).
- **Autonomy** — freedom to invest without first asking the government.

**Don't confuse** — A **statutory corporation** (born of a special Act, e.g. LIC) with a **government company** (registered under the Companies Act, e.g. SAIL). And the autonomy order is Miniratna < Navratna < Maharatna.

**Remember it** — Autonomy ladder: Mini → Nav → Maha (small jewel to great jewel).

**TL;DR**

- Three PSE types: departmental (Railways), statutory corporation (LIC), government company (SAIL, 51%+).
- Maharatna (2010): prior Navratna + net worth ≥ ₹15,000 cr, turnover ≥ ₹25,000 cr, net profit ≥ ₹5,000 cr.
- 2025 count: 14 Maharatnas, 26 Navratnas, 65 Miniratnas.
keyPoints: PSEs aim at growth in critical sectors, balanced regional development, employment and control of strategic sectors.
Three types: departmental undertaking (Railways), statutory corporation (LIC), government company (SAIL, ≥51% govt).
Maharatna (created 2010): prior Navratna status, net worth ≥ ₹15,000 cr, turnover ≥ ₹25,000 cr, net profit ≥ ₹5,000 cr.
Maharatna can invest up to 15% of net worth (cap ₹5,000 cr) without government approval.
As of 2025 there are 14 Maharatnas, 26 Navratnas and 65 Miniratnas.
items.mnemonic: Autonomy ladder: Miniratna → Navratna → Maharatna (small to great jewel).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Public Sector Enterprises; DPE guidelines 2025

items.title: MSMEs, Industrial Sickness & the IBC
items.body:
**In one line** — MSMEs are India's job-rich small-firm backbone, now defined by a combined investment-and-turnover rule, with the IBC giving a time-bound exit for failed firms.

**Why it is asked** — The 2025 revised MSME limits, the composite criterion and the IBC-2016 facts are directly examinable and current.

## The story — defining an MSME

- The **2020** revision (part of Atmanirbhar Bharat) did two things: it **removed the earlier distinction between manufacturing and service enterprises**, and it adopted a **composite criterion** combining investment in plant and machinery with annual turnover (a firm is judged on **both**).
- The limits were then **enhanced with effect from 1 April 2025**:

| Class (from 1 Apr 2025) | Investment | Turnover |
|---|---|---|
| Micro | up to ₹2.5 cr | up to ₹10 cr |
| Small | up to ₹25 cr | up to ₹100 cr |
| Medium | up to ₹125 cr | up to ₹500 cr |

## The story — significance and problems

- MSMEs contribute about **30% of GDP** and nearly **half of exports**, and are a major source of employment — the second-largest employer after agriculture.
- Their chronic, commonly faced problems: **inadequate (costly or scarce) credit, delayed payments, outdated technology, and weak marketing/infrastructure**.

## MSMEs in Andhra Pradesh

- In AP too, MSMEs are a major source of non-farm employment and industrial output in the state.
- The state provides incentives, MSME/industrial parks and single-desk clearances to support them.
- AP MSMEs are classified using the same composite investment-and-turnover criterion applicable nationally — states do not set their own MSME definitions.

## Industrial sickness and the IBC

- A 'sick' unit is one whose losses have eroded its net worth. The **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC)** gives a **time-bound** way to resolve or wind up such firms, replacing the slow old **SICA/BIFR** route.
- Company cases are decided by the **NCLT**; a **pre-packaged** insolvency option was added for MSMEs in 2021.

## Terms explained

- **Composite criterion** — classification using investment and turnover together.
- **Turnover** — total annual sales.
- **IBC / NCLT** — the 2016 insolvency law and the tribunal that decides company cases.

**Don't confuse** — An MSME is now judged by **both** investment **and** turnover (not investment alone), and the **manufacturing/service distinction was dropped** in 2020.

**Remember it** — 2025 limits double in a tidy ladder: Micro 10, Small 100, Medium 500 (turnover, in ₹ crore).

**TL;DR**

- 2020: composite investment-plus-turnover criterion, no manufacturing/service split.
- From 1 Apr 2025: Micro ≤ ₹2.5cr/₹10cr, Small ≤ ₹25cr/₹100cr, Medium ≤ ₹125cr/₹500cr.
- MSMEs ~30% of GDP, ~half of exports; problems = credit and delayed payments.
- IBC 2016: time-bound resolution via NCLT; replaced SICA/BIFR.
keyPoints: MSME uses a composite investment-plus-turnover criterion (2020), with no manufacturing/service distinction.
From 1 Apr 2025: Micro ≤ ₹2.5cr/₹10cr, Small ≤ ₹25cr/₹100cr, Medium ≤ ₹125cr/₹500cr (investment/turnover).
MSMEs contribute ~30% of GDP and nearly half of exports; key problems are credit shortage and delayed payments.
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 gives a time-bound resolution and replaced SICA/BIFR.
IBC cases for companies are adjudicated by the NCLT.
items.source: Ministry of MSME; Union Budget 2025-26; IBC 2016 / IBBI

items.title: Make in India, PLI & Startup/Standup India
items.body:
**In one line** — A family of schemes aims to lift manufacturing's share of GDP, reward home-made production and widen entrepreneurship.

**Why it is asked** — Launch years, the 14-sector PLI, the Startup-vs-Standup distinction and the Eight Core Industries list are classic exam fare.

## The story

- **Make in India (25 September 2014)** — a drive to make India a **global manufacturing hub**, originally across **25 sectors**, with the slogan **'Zero Defect, Zero Effect'**; it targets raising **manufacturing to about 25% of GDP**.
- **Production Linked Incentive (PLI, from 2020)** — pays a cash incentive as a **percentage of the extra (incremental) sales** of goods **made in India**, so firms are rewarded for producing *more* at home. It covers **14 sectors** including electronics/mobiles, pharmaceuticals, automobiles and components, telecom, textiles, food processing, solar PV and others) with a total outlay of about **₹1.97 lakh crore**, and is intended to **build domestic manufacturing capacity and reduce import dependence**.
- **Startup India (2016)** — promotes innovation-driven new enterprises; gives DPIIT recognition, tax breaks, easier compliance and a **Fund of Funds** to back innovation-led startups.
- **Standup India (2016)** — facilitates bank loans of **₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore** for at least one **SC/ST** borrower and one **woman** borrower per bank branch for a new (greenfield) enterprise.

## Eight Core Industries & the IIP

- The **eight core industries** are **Coal, Crude Oil, Natural Gas, Refinery Products, Fertilizers, Steel, Cement and Electricity**. Together they carry about **40.27% weight** in the **Index of Industrial Production (IIP)** (base year 2011-12). Among the eight, **Refinery Products has the largest single weight (~28%)**.

## Terms explained

- **Incremental sales** — the increase in sales over a base year, on which PLI is paid.
- **Greenfield enterprise** — a brand-new venture (not an expansion of an existing one).
- **IIP** — the monthly index of industrial output.

**Don't confuse** — **Startup India** (innovation-based startups) with **Standup India** (SC/ST and women entrepreneurs, ₹10 lakh-₹1 crore loans); both are 2016, not 2014.

**Remember it** — Core-8 hook: 'Come Come, Not Really For Some Cool Energy' — Coal, Crude oil, Natural gas, Refinery, Fertilizers, Steel, Cement, Electricity.

**TL;DR**

- Make in India (2014): 25 sectors, 'Zero Defect Zero Effect', ~25% manufacturing GDP target.
- PLI (2020): 14 sectors, ~₹1.97 lakh crore, rewards incremental domestic sales.
- Startup India + Standup India (both 2016).
- Eight Core = ~40.27% of IIP; Refinery Products the heaviest.
keyPoints: Make in India launched 25 Sep 2014, 25 sectors, 'Zero Defect Zero Effect', targets ~25% manufacturing GDP share.
PLI (2020) rewards incremental domestic sales across 14 sectors, outlay ~₹1.97 lakh crore.
Startup India (2016) offers DPIIT recognition, tax breaks and a Fund of Funds.
Standup India (2016) funds ₹10 lakh–₹1 crore loans for SC/ST and women entrepreneurs.
Eight Core Industries carry ~40.27% weight in the IIP (base 2011-12); Refinery Products has the largest single weight (~28%).
items.mnemonic: Core-8: 'Come Come, Not Really For Some Cool Energy' — Coal, Crude oil, Natural gas, Refinery, Fertilizers, Steel, Cement, Electricity.
items.source: DPIIT — Make in India, PLI, Startup India; DFS — Standup India; Office of Economic Adviser (IIP)

items.title: Industrial Corridors, Labour Codes & the AP Angle
items.body:
**In one line** — Big-ticket industrial geography (SEZs, NIMZs, corridors) plus the new four labour codes shape where and how factories grow — and Andhra Pradesh's coastal corridor is a leading case.

**Why it is asked** — SEZ/NIMZ/corridor definitions, the 21 Nov 2025 labour-code date, and the AP-specific VCIC/node facts are all examinable (and AP-weighted).

## The story — industrial infrastructure

- **SEZ (Special Economic Zone)** — a **duty-free enclave** treated as foreign territory for trade operations and tariffs; SEZs function under the **SEZ Act, 2005**.
- **NIMZ (National Investment and Manufacturing Zone)** — envisaged as a **large integrated industrial township** under the **National Manufacturing Policy, 2011**.
- **Corridors** — long industrial belts: **DMIC** (Delhi-Mumbai — India's first major industrial corridor project), CBIC, Amritsar-Kolkata, and the **East Coast Economic Corridor (ECEC)**.

## The story — four labour codes (2025)

- Four codes consolidate **29 central labour laws** into a single framework: the **Code on Wages, 2019**, and the **Industrial Relations Code**, **Code on Social Security** and **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code** (all 2020).
- They **came into force across the country on 21 November 2025**, extend social security to **gig and platform workers**, and standardise the definition of 'wages'.

## The story — Andhra Pradesh angle

- The **Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor (VCIC)** is the **first phase of the ECEC**, India's **first coastal economic corridor**. The **Asian Development Bank (ADB)** is the lead partner — the Visakhapatnam-Chennai corridor is developed with ADB support; the ~800 km corridor passes through several districts of Andhra Pradesh and is aligned broadly with the **Golden Quadrilateral** and supports the **Act East Policy**.
- The **AP Industrial Infrastructure Corporation (APIIC)** develops and manages industrial parks (and SEZs) in the state.
- AP's successive industrial policies seek to attract investment and generate employment through single-desk clearances and incentives. Industrial nodes promoted along the state's industrial framework and the Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor include **Sri City**, **Kopparthi (Kadapa)** and **Orvakal (Kurnool)**; AP is strong in ports, pharma and food processing.
- **SEZs in AP:** the **Visakhapatnam SEZ (VSEZ)** was among the earliest Central-government-promoted multi-product SEZs in India; **Sri City**, near the Andhra Pradesh-Tamil Nadu border in **Tirupati district**, is a large private multi-product industrial park/SEZ.

## AP ports, airport and mega-projects (status 2026)

| Port | What to know |
|---|---|
| **Visakhapatnam** | AP's only major (Central-government) port |
| **Krishnapatnam** | Privately developed all-weather deep-water port in Nellore district |
| **Gangavaram** | One of India's deepest ports, near Visakhapatnam |
| **Ramayapatnam** | New greenfield port being developed by the AP government (Prakasam district); targeted to be operational by **December 2026** |
| **Machilipatnam** | Greenfield port; targeted for **late 2026** |
| **Kakinada SEZ (Gateway) port** | Greenfield port; target **March 2028** |

- **Bhogapuram airport** — named **Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport**; located in **Vizianagaram district**; inaugurated in **August 2026**, with commercial operations beginning shortly after.
- **AM/NS integrated steel plant** (ArcelorMittal-Nippon Steel) — coming up at **Nakkapalli in Anakapalli district**; foundation stone laid in **March 2026**, production targeted around **2029**; planned capacity about **17.8 MTPA** (million tonnes per annum), with an initial phase of ~8.2 MTPA.
- **NTPC Green Energy Ltd (NGEL) green hydrogen hub** — described as India's largest, at **Pudimadaka, near Visakhapatnam**.
- **AI/data-centre hub, Visakhapatnam** — involves **Google along with the Adani group (and Airtel)**, investment of the order of **USD 15 billion**; planned as a **~1 GW data-centre campus**, described as among the largest single foreign investments in India; to be developed over roughly **2026-2030**.
- The state has cited investment **MoUs of the order of USD 175 billion** across several hundred projects (2026); anchor projects include the AM/NS steel plant, the NTPC green hydrogen hub and the Google-Adani AI data hub.

**Don't confuse** — Visakhapatnam is the *major* (Central) port; Gangavaram next to it is a *deep private* port; Krishnapatnam (Nellore) is private; Ramayapatnam (Prakasam) is the new *state* greenfield port.

## Terms explained

- **SEZ** — a tax/duty-free zone to boost exports.
- **Gig/platform workers** — app-based workers (delivery, ride-hailing) now covered by social security.
- **Golden Quadrilateral** — the highway network linking Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.

**Don't confuse** — **DMIC** is India's first *industrial* corridor; **VCIC/ECEC** is India's first *coastal* economic corridor. Both 'firsts', different senses.

**Remember it** — VCIC = 'Vizag-Chennai, coast, ADB' — AP's flagship corridor.

**TL;DR**

- SEZ (Act 2005) = duty-free enclave; NIMZ (2011) = integrated township; DMIC = first industrial corridor.
- Four labour codes consolidate 29 laws; in force 21 Nov 2025; cover gig workers.
- VCIC = first phase of ECEC (first coastal corridor), ADB-led, through AP; nodes Sri City, Kopparthi, Orvakal.
keyPoints: SEZs (SEZ Act 2005) are duty-free enclaves; NIMZs are integrated townships under the National Manufacturing Policy 2011.
DMIC (Delhi-Mumbai) was India's first flagship industrial corridor.
Four labour codes consolidate 29 central laws: Wages (2019), Industrial Relations, Social Security, OSH (all 2020).
The four labour codes came into force on 21 November 2025 and cover gig/platform workers.
VCIC is the first phase of the East Coast Economic Corridor (India's first coastal corridor), with ADB as lead partner, running through AP.
AP investment nodes include Sri City, Kopparthi (Kadapa) and Orvakal (Kurnool).
items.source: DPIIT/NICDC; Ministry of Labour & Employment (labour codes, 21 Nov 2025); ADB / Government of Andhra Pradesh — VCIC

items.title: Exam-Precision: Data Agencies, Standards Marks & Enterprise-Finance Schemes
items.body:
**In one line** — A set of precise 'who-does-what' facts that UPSC/APPSC like to test with tricky distractors.

**Why it is asked** — These are pure discrimination questions: the right agency, the right certifying body, the right scheme purpose.

## The story — who compiles what?

| Body | Function (the exam trigger) |
|---|---|
| **Labour Bureau** (Ministry of Labour & Employment) | Compiles data on **industrial disputes, closures, retrenchments and lay-offs** in factories; also the CPI for Industrial Workers. Not the CSO or DPIIT |
| **Coal Controller's Organization (CCO)** | A major source of **coal statistics**; monitors **captive coal/lignite block** development; hears objections to acquiring coal-bearing areas. It does **not** guarantee timely delivery of coal |
| **NSO/MoSPI** | Compiles the **Index of Industrial Production (IIP)** |

## The story — standards marks

- The **BIS ISI mark** is **mandatory** for products such as **automotive tyres and tubes**.
- **AGMARK** is issued by the **Directorate of Marketing & Inspection (DMI), Ministry of Agriculture** — not by the FAO.

## The story — Eight Core Industries weights

- Among the eight, **Refinery Products carries the highest weight (~28.04%)**, followed by **Electricity (~19.85%)** and **Steel (~17.92%)**. (So if an exam option set omits Refinery, Electricity is the heaviest of those listed.) The eight together are **~40.27% of the IIP**.

## The story — enterprise-finance & turnaround schemes

| Scheme | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **PM MUDRA Yojana (2015)** | Bring **micro/small entrepreneurs into the formal financial system** (loan tiers Shishu/Kishore/Tarun) |
| **Stand Up India** | Entrepreneurship among **SC/ST and women**; **refinanced via SIDBI** |
| **UDAY (2015)** | **Financial turnaround of power distribution companies (DISCOMs)** |
| **S4A (2016)** | An **RBI** scheme to rework the finances of large stressed corporates |
| **Small Finance Banks** | Credit to **small business units and small & marginal farmers** (financial inclusion) |

## Terms explained

- **AGMARK** — a quality mark for agricultural produce (from DMI, not the FAO).
- **DISCOM** — an electricity distribution company.
- **Captive block** — a coal/mineral block earmarked for a company's own use.

**Don't confuse** — The **Labour Bureau** (industrial-dispute data), **not** the CSO/DPIIT; **AGMARK = DMI**, not FAO; among the eight core, **Refinery (not Electricity) is the single heaviest**.

**Remember it** — Agency hooks: Labour disputes → Labour Bureau; Coal numbers → Coal Controller; Farm-produce grade → AGMARK.

**TL;DR**

- Labour Bureau = industrial-dispute data; CCO = coal statistics; NSO = IIP.
- BIS/ISI mandatory for tyres & tubes; AGMARK by DMI (not FAO).
- Eight core: Refinery heaviest (~28%), then Electricity (~19.85%); eight = ~40.27% of IIP.
- MUDRA (formalise micro-firms), Stand Up India (SC/ST & women, SIDBI), UDAY (DISCOMs), S4A (RBI stressed assets), SFBs (small units & farmers).
keyPoints: The Labour Bureau compiles data on industrial disputes, closures, retrenchments and lay-offs (not the CSO or DPIIT).
The Coal Controller's Organization is a major source of coal statistics and monitors captive coal/lignite block development.
The BIS ISI mark is mandatory for automotive tyres and tubes; AGMARK is issued by the Directorate of Marketing & Inspection (Ministry of Agriculture), not the FAO.
Among the Eight Core Industries, Refinery Products carries the highest weight (~28%), followed by Electricity (~19.85%); the eight together are about 40.27% of the IIP.
PM MUDRA formalises micro-entrepreneurs; Stand Up India (SC/ST & women) is refinanced through SIDBI; UDAY revives DISCOMs; S4A is an RBI stressed-asset scheme.
Small Finance Banks provide credit to small business units and small & marginal farmers.
items.source: PIB; RBI; Ministry of Labour (Labour Bureau); Ministry of Coal (CCO); BIS; Office of the Economic Adviser (IIP weights); UPSC PYQ pattern

items.title: Industrial History, Policy Timeline, Plans & Labour Laws
items.body:
**In one line:** modern Indian industry began with mills in the 1850s, was steered by a chain of policy documents from 1948 to 1991, and is governed by labour laws now folded into four codes.

**Why it is asked:** "first mill / first steel plant", "which policy created the joint sector / DICs", UPSC 2019 on Plans and UPSC 2017 on the Trade Disputes Act are direct questions.

## Firsts of Indian industry

**The story**

| First | Year / place |
|---|---|
| Cotton mill | **1854, Bombay** (Cowasji Nanabhai Davar) |
| Jute mill | **1855, Rishra** (Bengal) |
| Cement | **1904, Madras** |
| TISCO steel | **1907, Jamshedpur** |

## Policy timeline

| Year | Policy / law | Point |
|---|---|---|
| **1948** | Industrial Policy Resolution | First policy; mixed economy |
| **1951** | **Industries (Development and Regulation) Act** | Legal basis of industrial **licensing** |
| **1956** | IPR 1956 | **Schedule A = 17** state industries, **Schedule B = 12**, Schedule C rest |
| **1967** | Reservation for small-scale industry | Items reserved for SSIs — all **de-reserved by 2015** |
| **1969** | **MRTP Act** | Curbed monopolies; replaced by the Competition Act |
| **1973** | Industrial Policy Statement; **FERA** | Introduced the **joint sector**; FERA replaced by **FEMA (1999)** |
| **1977** | Industrial Policy Statement | Small sector; **District Industries Centres (1978)** |
| **1991** | New Industrial Policy (**24 July 1991**) | Delicensing, LPG |
| **2002** | **Competition Act** | **Competition Commission of India** |

## Industry in the Plans (UPSC 2019)

- From the **Second Plan** there was a determined thrust towards substituting basic and **capital goods** industries (the **Mahalanobis** model).
- The **Fourth Plan** aimed at correcting the earlier trend of increased **concentration of wealth** and economic power.
- The Fifth Plan did **not** "first include the financial sector" — that statement was false.

## Two growth concepts (UPSC 2015, 2018)

- A **high capital-output ratio** means saving and capital formation may not raise output much.
- Replacing wooden ploughs with **steel** ploughs is **capital-augmenting** technological progress.

## Labour laws

| Law | Point |
|---|---|
| **Trade Unions Act, 1926** | Registration of trade unions |
| **Trade Disputes Act, 1929** | Courts/tribunals and a ban on strikes in public utilities without notice (UPSC 2017) |
| **Industrial Disputes Act, 1947** | Strikes, lay-offs, retrenchment |
| **Factories Act, 1948** | Health and safety in factories |

- These and other laws — **29** central laws — were merged into four codes in force from **21 November 2025**: **Code on Wages (2019)**, **Industrial Relations Code**, **Code on Social Security** and **OSH Code** (2020).
- The **Labour Bureau** (Ministry of Labour) compiles industrial-dispute data and the **CPI-IW**.

**Don't confuse** — *IDRA 1951* (licensing law) with *IPR 1956* (policy schedules); *1973* (joint sector, FERA) with *1977* (DICs, small sector).

**TL;DR**
- Cotton mill 1854 Bombay; jute 1855 Rishra; cement 1904 Madras; TISCO 1907.
- IPR 1948; IDRA 1951; IPR 1956 (A 17, B 12); SSI reservation 1967 → nil 2015; MRTP 1969; 1973 joint sector + FERA; 1977 DICs; NIP 24 July 1991; FEMA 1999; Competition Act 2002.
- Second Plan capital goods; Fourth Plan against concentration of wealth.
- High capital-output ratio; steel plough = capital-augmenting.
- Trade Unions 1926, Trade Disputes 1929, ID Act 1947, Factories 1948 → 4 codes from 21 Nov 2025.
keyPoints: India's first cotton mill: 1854, Bombay (Cowasji Nanabhai Davar); first jute mill: 1855, Rishra.
India's first cement factory: 1904, Madras; TISCO: 1907, Jamshedpur.
The Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 is the legal basis of industrial licensing.
IPR 1956: Schedule A had 17 industries and Schedule B had 12.
Reservation of items for small-scale industries began in 1967; all items were de-reserved by 2015.
MRTP Act 1969 curbed monopolies and was replaced by the Competition Act, 2002 (Competition Commission of India).
Industrial Policy Statement 1973 introduced the joint sector; FERA 1973 was replaced by FEMA 1999.
Industrial Policy Statement 1977 stressed small industry and set up District Industries Centres (1978).
The New Industrial Policy was announced on 24 July 1991.
The pre-1991 licensing regime is popularly called the 'Licence-Permit Raj'; the 1991 policy followed a balance-of-payments crisis.
From the Second Plan there was a determined thrust towards substitution of basic and capital goods industries; the Fourth Plan aimed at correcting concentration of wealth (UPSC 2019).
A high capital-output ratio means capital formation may not raise output much (UPSC 2018).
Replacing wooden ploughs with steel ploughs is capital-augmenting technological progress (UPSC 2015).
Trade Unions Act 1926; Trade Disputes Act 1929 provided tribunals and a ban on strikes (UPSC 2017); Industrial Disputes Act 1947; Factories Act 1948.
The four labour codes merged 29 central laws and came into force on 21 November 2025.
The Labour Bureau compiles industrial-dispute data and the CPI-IW.

items.title: PSEs in 2026 — Ratna Updates, Steel Plants, Disinvestment & New PSE Policy
items.body:
**In one line:** the Ratna club keeps growing (14 Maharatnas, 29 Navratnas by mid-2026), the big steel PSUs have foreign-aided origins, and disinvestment moved from a 1990s commission to DIPAM and the 2021 New PSE Policy.

**Why it is asked:** "who is the 14th Maharatna / latest Navratna", "which steel plant was built with whose help" and "which body handles disinvestment" are favourites.

## Ratna status — history and 2026 position

**The story**

| Grade | Introduced | Latest count / addition |
|---|---|---|
| **Navratna** and **Miniratna** | **1997** | **29** Navratnas — **Chennai Petroleum (28th)** and **Garden Reach Shipbuilders (GRSE, 29th)** in **June 2026** |
| **Maharatna** | **2009-10** | **14** — **Hindustan Aeronautics (HAL)** became the **14th** in **October 2024**; **Oil India** was the 13th (2023) |
| **Miniratna Category-I** | 1997 | e.g. **MECON** (2026) |

- **Maharatnas** (source list): BHEL, BPCL, Coal India, GAIL, HPCL, IOCL, NTPC, ONGC, PFC, POWERGRID, SAIL, REC, Oil India, HAL.
- **Navratna** autonomy: up to **₹1,000 crore** (or 15% of net worth) per project without approval; needs a score of **60/100**.
- **RINL** (Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd, Visakhapatnam, 1982) is a **Navratna**; the Cabinet approved a **₹11,440 crore revival plan** for it in **January 2025**.

## PSE types — source examples

- **Departmental undertaking:** Indian Railways, India Post. **Statutory corporation:** LIC (the source also lists ONGC). **Government company:** BHEL, SAIL, NTPC.

## Steel plants and their foreign partners

| Plant | State | Partner |
|---|---|---|
| **Bhilai** | Chhattisgarh | **USSR** |
| **Rourkela** | Odisha | **West Germany** |
| **Durgapur** | West Bengal | **United Kingdom** |
| **Bokaro** | Jharkhand | **USSR** |
| **Visakhapatnam (RINL)** | Andhra Pradesh | Shore-based plant; first coastal integrated steel plant |

## Disinvestment

| Step | Year |
|---|---|
| **C. Rangarajan Committee** on disinvestment | **1993** |
| **Disinvestment Commission** (G.V. Ramakrishna) | **1996** |
| Department of Disinvestment | **1999** → renamed **DIPAM** in **2016** |
| **New PSE Policy** — strategic vs non-strategic sectors | **2021** |
| **Air India** handed to the **Tata** group | **27 January 2022** |

- The **New PSE Policy (2021)** keeps a **bare minimum** presence in **four strategic sectors** — atomic energy, space and defence; transport and telecom; power, petroleum, coal and minerals; banking, insurance and financial services — and aims to privatise or close PSEs elsewhere.

**Don't confuse** — *Disinvestment* (selling part of the government's shares) with *strategic sale* (handing over management control, as with Air India).

**TL;DR**
- Navratna/Miniratna 1997; Maharatna 2009-10; 14 Maharatnas (HAL 14th, Oct 2024); 29 Navratnas (CPCL 28th, GRSE 29th, June 2026).
- RINL Vizag Navratna; ₹11,440 crore revival (Jan 2025).
- Bhilai and Bokaro USSR; Rourkela West Germany; Durgapur UK.
- Rangarajan 1993; Disinvestment Commission 1996; DoD 1999 → DIPAM 2016; New PSE Policy 2021 (4 strategic sectors); Air India to Tata 27 Jan 2022.
keyPoints: Navratna and Miniratna status were introduced in 1997; Maharatna in 2009-10.
HAL became the 14th Maharatna in October 2024; Oil India was the 13th (2023).
Chennai Petroleum (28th) and Garden Reach Shipbuilders (29th) became Navratnas in June 2026.
Navratnas can invest up to ₹1,000 crore per project without approval and need a score of 60/100.
RINL (Visakhapatnam, 1982) is a Navratna; the Cabinet approved an ₹11,440 crore revival plan in January 2025.
Navratna NMDC is headquartered at Hyderabad and NALCO at Bhubaneswar.
Bhilai and Bokaro steel plants were built with USSR help, Rourkela with West Germany, Durgapur with the United Kingdom.
C. Rangarajan Committee on disinvestment 1993; Disinvestment Commission (G.V. Ramakrishna) 1996.
Department of Disinvestment (1999) was renamed DIPAM in 2016.
New PSE Policy (2021) keeps a bare minimum presence in four strategic sectors and privatises the rest.
Air India was handed to the Tata group on 27 January 2022 (strategic sale).

items.title: IIP & Core Index (2022-23 Base), MSME Law & Enterprise Finance
items.body:
**In one line:** in 2026 India rebased its industrial indices to 2022-23 (and added iron ore as a ninth core industry), while MSMEs are served by a 2006 law, Udyam registration and a ladder of credit schemes.

**Why it is asked:** the base-year change and "nine core industries" are fresh current affairs; MUDRA tiers, PM Vishwakarma and SIDBI are perennial.

## Index of Industrial Production (IIP)

- Compiled by the **NSO (MoSPI)**. The **new series with base 2022-23** was released on **1 June 2026** (data for April 2026) — the **10th** revision; the first IIP had base **1937**, and the previous base was **2011-12**.
- It gives separate indices for **renewable and non-renewable electricity** and splits mining into fuel, metallic (including **rare earth**) and non-metallic minerals.

## Index of Core Industries (ICI)

**The story**

| Feature | Old series (base 2011-12) | New series (base 2022-23, released **20 July 2026**) |
|---|---|---|
| Industries | **Eight** | **Nine** — **iron ore** added |
| Weight in IIP | **40.27%** | **32.88%** |
| Heaviest | **Refinery products (~28%)**, then electricity (~19.85%), steel (~17.92%) | Iron ore carries about **4.9%** |

- The changes follow a committee under **Praveen Mahto** (November 2025). The ICI is released by the **Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT**.

## MSME law and support

| Item | Point |
|---|---|
| **MSMED Act** | **2006** — the legal definition of MSMEs |
| **Udyam registration** | From **1 July 2020** — online, paperless |
| **SIDBI** | **1990**, HQ **Lucknow** — apex MSME finance; refinances Stand-Up India |
| **CGTMSE** | **2000** — collateral-free credit guarantees |
| **45-day rule** | Buyers must pay MSMEs within **45 days** (MSMED Act; tax deduction denied otherwise under section 43B(h), 2023) |
| **TReDS** | Online platform to discount MSME invoices |

## MUDRA (launched 8 April 2015)

| Tier | Loan size |
|---|---|
| **Shishu** | up to **₹50,000** |
| **Kishore** | up to **₹5 lakh** |
| **Tarun** | up to **₹10 lakh** |
| **Tarun Plus** | **₹10-20 lakh** (Budget 2024-25) |

## PM Vishwakarma

- Launched **17 September 2023** for artisans in **18 trades** with about **₹13,000 crore**; it crossed **30 lakh registrations** by its third anniversary (September 2026).

**Don't confuse** — *IIP* (NSO/MoSPI) with *ICI* (Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT). And the old "eight core" and 40.27% figures belong to the **2011-12** series.

**TL;DR**
- IIP new base 2022-23 (1 June 2026), 10th revision, first base 1937.
- ICI base 2022-23 (20 July 2026): nine industries with iron ore (4.9%), 32.88% of IIP; old eight = 40.27%, refinery heaviest.
- MSMED Act 2006; Udyam 1 July 2020; SIDBI 1990 Lucknow; CGTMSE 2000; 45-day payment rule.
- MUDRA 8 April 2015: Shishu ₹50,000, Kishore ₹5 lakh, Tarun ₹10 lakh, Tarun Plus ₹20 lakh.
- PM Vishwakarma 17 Sep 2023, 18 trades, ₹13,000 crore.
keyPoints: IIP is compiled by the NSO (MoSPI); a new series with base 2022-23 was released on 1 June 2026, the 10th revision (first base 1937, previous 2011-12).
The new IIP has separate indices for renewable and non-renewable electricity and includes rare earth minerals in metallic mining.
The new Index of Core Industries (base 2022-23, released 20 July 2026) has nine industries after adding iron ore.
The nine core industries carry 32.88% weight in the IIP; the old eight carried 40.27%.
In the 2011-12 core series refinery products had the largest weight (~28%), then electricity (~19.85%) and steel (~17.92%).
Iron ore carries about 4.9% weight in the new core index; the revision followed the Praveen Mahto committee (Nov 2025).
The ICI is released by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT.
MSMED Act 2006; Udyam registration from 1 July 2020.
MSMEs contribute about 30% of GDP and nearly half of exports; under the IBC, insolvency cases of companies are adjudicated by the NCLT.
SIDBI (1990, Lucknow) is the apex MSME finance body; CGTMSE (2000) gives collateral-free guarantees.
Buyers must pay MSMEs within 45 days; section 43B(h) (2023) denies the tax deduction otherwise; TReDS discounts MSME invoices.
MUDRA (8 April 2015): Shishu up to ₹50,000, Kishore up to ₹5 lakh, Tarun up to ₹10 lakh, Tarun Plus up to ₹20 lakh.
PM Vishwakarma (17 September 2023): 18 trades, about ₹13,000 crore, over 30 lakh registrations by September 2026.

items.title: Manufacturing Push 2020-26 — PLI, Semiconductors, Parks & Smart Cities — and AP Industry
items.body:
**In one line:** after 2020 India layered PLI, a semiconductor mission, component schemes, textile parks and industrial smart cities on top of Make in India — and Andhra Pradesh landed some of the biggest projects.

**Why it is asked:** outlays and "which state got which park / smart city" are current-affairs MCQs; AP mega-projects are APPSC-specific.

## National schemes

**The story**

| Scheme | Year | Key numbers |
|---|---|---|
| **National Manufacturing Policy** | **2011** | Manufacturing to **25%** of GDP and **100 million** jobs; created **NIMZs** |
| **PLI** (14 sectors) | 2020 | **₹1.97 lakh crore**; **₹28,748 crore** disbursed by December 2025 |
| **India Semiconductor Mission** | **December 2021** | **₹76,000 crore**; **ISM 2.0** announced in Budget 2026-27 |
| **Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme (ECMS)** | 2025 | ₹22,919 crore, raised to **₹40,000 crore** in Budget 2026-27 |
| **National Manufacturing Mission** | Budget **2025-26** | Umbrella mission, including clean-tech manufacturing |
| **PM MITRA** textile parks | 2023 | **7** parks (one at **Warangal**, Telangana) |
| **Industrial smart cities** (NICDP) | **August 2024** | **12** cities, **₹28,602 crore**; AP got **two — Orvakal and Kopparthy** |

- **Kandla** (1965) was **Asia's first Export Processing Zone**; EPZs became SEZs under the **SEZ Act, 2005**.

## Andhra Pradesh industry, 2024-26

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **AP Industrial Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29)** | Released with five other policies in **October 2024**; target **₹30 lakh crore** investment and **20 lakh** jobs |
| **BPCL refinery** | **9 MMTPA** refinery-cum-petrochemical complex near **Ramayapatnam** port, about **₹1,03,408 crore**, on 5,200 acres (environmental clearance recommended, Oct 2026) |
| **AM/NS steel plant** | **Nakkapalli** (Anakapalli); **17.8 MTPA**; foundation **23 March 2026** |
| **NTPC Green Hydrogen Hub** | **Pudimadaka** (Visakhapatnam); about **₹1.85 lakh crore**; foundation **8 January 2025** |
| **Google AI data hub** | **Visakhapatnam**; about **$15 billion**, **1 GW** — the largest single FDI in India |
| **Kia Motors plant** | **Penukonda**, Anantapur (2019) |
| **Industry's share** | About **21%** of AP's GSDP (2024-25) |

**Don't confuse** — *Orvakal* (Kurnool) and *Kopparthy* (Kadapa) are AP's industrial smart cities; *Warangal* (Telangana), not AP, has the PM MITRA park.

**TL;DR**
- NMP 2011: 25% of GDP, 100 million jobs, NIMZ.
- PLI ₹1.97 lakh cr (₹28,748 cr paid by Dec 2025); ISM ₹76,000 cr (Dec 2021), ISM 2.0; ECMS ₹40,000 cr.
- PM MITRA 7 parks; 12 smart cities (Aug 2024, ₹28,602 cr) incl. Orvakal and Kopparthy; Kandla first EPZ 1965.
- AP policy 4.0 (2024-29): ₹30 lakh cr, 20 lakh jobs; BPCL 9 MMTPA Ramayapatnam; AM/NS Nakkapalli 17.8 MTPA; NTPC H2 Pudimadaka; Google $15 bn Vizag; Kia Penukonda; industry ~21% of GSDP.
keyPoints: National Manufacturing Policy 2011: manufacturing to 25% of GDP and 100 million jobs; created NIMZs.
PLI covers 14 sectors with ₹1.97 lakh crore; ₹28,748 crore had been disbursed by December 2025.
Make in India was launched on 25 September 2014 with the slogan 'Zero Defect, Zero Effect'; Startup India (2016) gives DPIIT recognition, tax breaks and a Fund of Funds.
India Semiconductor Mission (December 2021) has ₹76,000 crore; ISM 2.0 was announced in Budget 2026-27.
The Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme outlay was raised from ₹22,919 crore to ₹40,000 crore in Budget 2026-27.
The National Manufacturing Mission was announced in Budget 2025-26.
PM MITRA: 7 mega textile parks, one at Warangal (Telangana).
In August 2024 the Cabinet approved 12 industrial smart cities (₹28,602 crore); Andhra Pradesh got Orvakal and Kopparthy.
Kandla (1965) was Asia's first Export Processing Zone.
AP Industrial Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29), released October 2024, targets ₹30 lakh crore investment and 20 lakh jobs.
BPCL is setting up a 9 MMTPA refinery-cum-petrochemical complex near Ramayapatnam port at about ₹1,03,408 crore.
AM/NS integrated steel plant at Nakkapalli (Anakapalli): 17.8 MTPA, foundation 23 March 2026.
NTPC Green Hydrogen Hub at Pudimadaka (Visakhapatnam): about ₹1.85 lakh crore, foundation 8 January 2025.
Google AI data hub at Visakhapatnam: about $15 billion, 1 GW — the largest single FDI in India.
Kia Motors' plant is at Penukonda, Anantapur (2019); industry is about 21% of AP's GSDP.

items.title: For Mains — Industry & Industrial Policy
items.body:
**In one line** — For Mains Paper-IV, industry is argued as a story of policy shift (control → liberalise → facilitate) and a jobs-and-manufacturing challenge, with Andhra Pradesh's corridor-and-mega-project push as the case.

**Why it is asked** — Syllabus clauses M4-9 (industrial development & policy — 1991 policy, PSUs, disinvestment, MSME, Make in India, SEZ, NIMZ), M4-10 (AP industrial policy — incentives, corridors, SEZs, power) and M4-11 (infrastructure — transport, energy, PPP).

## The dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| **Evolution** | IPR 1948 → 1956 ('economic constitution') → NIP 1991 (delicensing, FDI, de-reservation 17→8→2) |
| **Reforms** | Disinvestment/DIPAM, IBC 2016, four labour codes (29→4, in force 21 Nov 2025), Competition Act 2002 |
| **Manufacturing push** | Make in India (~25% GDP target), PLI (14 sectors, ₹1.97 lakh cr), MSME revamp, Startup/Standup |
| **Infrastructure** | SEZ/NIMZ, corridors (DMIC, ECEC/VCIC), ports, energy, PPP |
| **Limitations** | Jobless growth, stagnant ~17% manufacturing share, regional imbalance, land/power/skilling gaps |
| **Way forward** | Deepen PLI linkages, ease factor markets (land/labour/credit), cluster & corridor-led growth, green manufacturing |

## Data, reports and schemes to quote

- Reserved public-sector industries **17 (1956) → 8 (1991) → 2** today.
- PLI **₹1.97 lakh crore / 14 sectors**; MSME ~30% of GDP, ~half of exports.
- Four labour codes consolidate **29 laws** (in force **21 Nov 2025**); **IBC 2016**; **14 Maharatnas** (2025).

## The AP angle

- **VCIC** (first phase of the ECEC, India's first coastal corridor, ADB-led); nodes **Sri City, Kopparthi, Orvakal**; APIIC as developer; single-desk clearances.
- Mega-projects: **AM/NS steel (Nakkapalli)**, **NTPC green hydrogen (Pudimadaka)**, **Google-Adani AI data hub (Visakhapatnam)**; greenfield ports (Ramayapatnam, Machilipatnam) and **Bhogapuram airport**; AP's claimed ~USD 175 bn MoUs.

## Use in answers

- **Example:** use VCIC + Pudimadaka green-hydrogen hub to argue that corridor-anchored, clean-energy manufacturing is AP's comparative advantage.
- **Quote:** the 1991 shift of the state 'from producer to facilitator and regulator'.
- **Diagram idea:** a timeline arrow 1948 → 1956 → 1991 → 2014 (Make in India) → 2020 (PLI) → 2025 (labour codes).

**TL;DR** — Frame industry as liberalisation + manufacturing + jobs + infrastructure; quote de-reservation 17→8→2, PLI ₹1.97 lakh cr, 29→4 labour codes (21 Nov 2025); use AP's VCIC and marquee projects (steel, green H2, AI hub) as the case study.
keyPoints: Mains clauses: M4-9 (industrial development & policy), M4-10 (AP industrial policy), M4-11 (infrastructure); Paper-IV.
Argue evolution (1948→1956→1991) → reforms (disinvestment, IBC, labour codes) → manufacturing push → infrastructure → limits → way forward.
Quote: de-reservation 17→8→2, PLI ₹1.97 lakh cr/14 sectors, 29→4 labour codes (21 Nov 2025), MSME ~30% GDP.
AP case: VCIC (first coastal corridor, ADB), Sri City/Kopparthi/Orvakal, AM/NS steel, NTPC green H2, Google-Adani AI hub, ~USD 175 bn MoUs.
Way forward: deepen PLI, ease land/labour/credit markets, corridor-and-cluster growth, green manufacturing.
